newsitem.title: UK: IPE gas oil seen revisiting 5-year highs if cold.
newsitem.headline: IPE gas oil seen revisiting 5-year highs if cold.

text.p: IPE gas oil futures are expected to revisit their five-year highs as European consumers fill up their tanks ahead of winter and last-minute logistical wrinkles are ironed out for Europe's new mandated diesel specifications.

Tight stocks in the Atlantic basin are forcing Europe and the U.S. to compete for scarce heating oil supplies and have exacerbated a steep backwardation on the IPE that discouraged building of inventories, traders and analysts said.

But prices are expected to cool off, barring a bone-chilling fourth quarter, once primary inventories are replenished and the October 1 European Union deadline passes for changing the sulphur content of diesel, they said.

Peter Bogin, associate director of Cambridge Energy Research Associates in Paris, credited gas oil's rally primarily to low inventories and said European refiners were well prepared for the diesel change.

"We're still living with the winter of last year...and then there was tremendous hesitation by refiners to build inventories as prices have been in backwardation and refiners are trying to cut costs and that means holding lower inventories," said Peter Bogin, associate director of Cambridge Energy Research Associates in Paris.
"Consumers meanwhile were waiting for prices to come off in the summer," he said.

But distillate stocks appear to be moving to secondary and tertiary levels which may back up primary stocks to more comfortable levels by mid- to late-October, if temperatures in the fourth quarter turn out normal or higher, he said.

IPE gas oil rallied about 33 percent since late July to touch a five-year high of $226.75 a tonne Sept 12. The spot Oct contract on Monday was trading at $215.50, with the Oct/Nov backwardation narrowing by about 50 cents to $6.50.

The European gas oil pool, which until now was 0.2 percent sulphur for both heating oil and diesel, will be split into about 60 pct 0.2 pct for heating oil and 40 percent 0.05 pct sulphur for diesel. The IPE will continue to specify 0.2 pct.

"Gas oil demand is likely to be strong in the near term because of low stocks in Germany...and because the U.S. market will inevitably call on European refiners to meet at least a part of the additional demand in the coming months," oil analysts at Kleinwort Benson said in a report.
European middle distillates stocks rose 3.75 million barrels in August from July, but at 286.28 million are still 25.79 million under a year ago, according to the Euroilstock Foundation.
Stocks in Germany, which eats about 30 percent of European demand, were 85.5 million, off from 89.86 million a year ago.
Middle distillate output rose 26,000 barrels per day in August to 5.209 million bpd, up 0.6 pct from a year ago.
"It's a price spike but there is a fundamental reason for it," said Leo Drollas, deputy director of the Centre for Global Energy Studies in London. "Worrying, I'd call it."
The expected arrival of at least 400,000 tonnes of North American gas oil to Europe in the beginning of October is expected to provide little relief.
"Both markets are in tight supply so if one is supplying the other the oil still has to come from somewhere...It's like robbing Peter to pay Paul," said one Swiss oil trader.
"We're likely to be open to some very big spikes if we see some very cold weather coming in," he added.

He also said German demand was running at a steady clip even though weakness in the mark has made prices more expensive than in recent years. Demand could even quicken if cooler weather prevails and those users holding out for lower prices must jump into the market, he said.

Charles Gray, energy analyst at Prudential Bache Futures, said that "...there is a general concern that there might be some competition between the U.S. and Europeans for what seems to be a limited supply of gas oil" and as long as NYMEX heating oil remains strong, gas oil could rally to the mid-$220s.
"But we would have to have a new factor introduced to get us beyond those levels, like cold weather or military activity (in the Middle East)."
-- London Newsroom, +44 171 542 8185
